In a recent development, arXiv:2611.21681v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: For a time $t_{c}$ of calculation in an $N$ qubit quantum computer that is much shorter than the intrinsic Heisenberg time $t_H$, $t_c\ll t_H$, the dynamics of the system is effectively irreversible and the couplings between the qubits give rise to a relaxation time scale $\tau_r$. If $t_H\gg t_c >\sim \tau_r$ one looses quantum coherence exponentially fast. Since $t_H$ scales exponentially with $N$ there is a threshold $N_c$ such that for $N\gg N_c$ one must be aware of possible intrinsic relaxation during calculation. As an order of magnitude estimation we find $N_c\approx \ln(\tau_r/T)$ where $T$ is a typical system specific oscillation time of a single qubit. $\tau_r$ can be estimated as the typical inverse transition rate between two parts of the system, one of which is treated as an environment of the other.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2509.15280v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trials (PCRCTs), healthcare providers are randomized, but intervention delivery and patient receipt may vary after assignment. In many PCRCTs, cluster-level implementation is measured using continuous implementation metrics, while individual compliance is recorded as a binary indicator. Standard complier average causal effect (CACE) estimands focus on individual-level compliance and do not account for heterogeneity in implementation across clusters. When intervention uptake is shaped by both cluster- and individual-level processes, it is of scientific interest to characterize how effects vary across these sources of compliance. We propose a Bayesian framework for PCRCTs with one-sided binary noncompliance at the individual level and one-sided partial compliance at the cluster level. The method uses a latent mixture model to summarize heterogeneity in cluster-level implementation based on baseline characteristics and treatment-arm implementation measures, and links these latent implementation strata to individual compliance and outcomes through a joint model. Because individual compliance and treatment-defined implementation measures are observed only under treatment assignment, the model imputes these quantities for control clusters and individuals assigned to control. The framework enables estimation of finite- and super-population intent-to-treat (ITT) and CACE estimands, both marginally and within latent implementation strata. We apply the method to the METRIcAL trial, a pragmatic cluster randomized study evaluating a personalized music intervention for nursing home residents with dementia. The analysis illustrates how accounting for implementation heterogeneity and individual compliance can provide insights beyond standard ITT analyses.

However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion. Code available at https://github.com/NVlabs/TTCov.

Temporal and spatial targets are shared across prompt families, while the non-physics families use deterministic family-appropriate semantic a_what targets derived from the same record. Across models and prompt families, physics remains the strongest regime overall, vstar_like is the clearest non-physics semantic comparison, and neutral_rstr behaves as a harder templated control. Prompt-family robustness is selective rather than universal, perturbation gains cluster in weak original cases, and spatial grounding is the weakest across settings. These results suggest that video Q&A reasoning benchmarks shall report physically grounded, prompt-aware, and perturbation-aware diagnostics alongside aggregate accuracy.

arXiv:2611.22198v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space. In a regression problem, if the regression function $f_0$ is inhomogeneous --- varying rapidly in one region, while being nearly flat in another --- no single model can be appropriate everywhere, and the fit degrades where the function varies most rapidly. Here we study an alternative in which, instead of fitting the network globally, we fit it locally. For each query point $x$, a \emph{local neural network} is trained on the $k$ nearest-neighbours of $x$ alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent. We analyze the performance of the resulting estimator through a localization approach, establishing that the pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of $k$ attains the rate $n^{-2\alpha/(2\alpha+d^{*})}$, up to logarithmic factors, when $f_0$ is locally $\alpha$-H\"older with $\alpha\in(0,1]$ and the covariates are supported on a $d^{*}$-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal. However, the local rate-optimality requires $k$ to be calibrated to the smoothness of $f_0$, which is unknown in practice. We therefore provide a locally adaptive choice of $k$ that makes the neural network adapt to the local H\"older exponent of $f_0$ and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously, both of which are potentially varying over the covariate domain. An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.

These predictions are used to construct a physics-informed Gibbs prior that both selects a small state-dependent candidate set and reweights policy logits before action selection. These results show that our method provides an effective mechanism for topology control in power grids.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22096v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce COSI (COnfidence from Scale Invariance), a framework for constructing confidence sets for statistical functionals. COSI builds on the HulC (Hull-based Confidence), which uses median unbiasedness to construct confidence sets from batch estimates. COSI uses scale-invariance properties shared by many common estimators. We divide the data into batches, compute an estimate in each batch, and retain each candidate parameter value for which the batch estimates pass a test of scale invariance. The resulting confidence sets are asymptotically valid under weaker assumptions than classical Wald and bootstrap procedures require, and their coverage can be closer to the nominal level in small samples. Applications include robust inference for the mean, regression coefficients in misspecified linear models, tensor norms, and Fr\'echet means.

Second, the ASA module learns the interactions between the spatiotemporal multi-scale queries. The entire model employs a backbone network and a feature pyramid network (FPN) as the encoder, then introduces a YOLOX and a DepthNet as a ROI\_Head to produce CQ, and repeatedly utilizes ASA and MSHS as the decoder to gain detection features. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes, Waymo, and Argoverse benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our CAM3DNet, and most existing camera-based 3D object detection methods are outperformed. The choice of information policy in such an environment reduces to an optimization over distributions of posterior means dominated by the prior in convex order. We study extreme points of this feasible set using results on irreducible-component structure from martingale transport theory. When the prior assigns zero mass to the union of the relative boundaries of the non-singleton components, then on each such component the distribution of posterior means is dominated by the prior in convex order. In such cases, extreme points must satisfy affine independence of the conditional posterior-mean support in almost every component. Without boundary negligibility, local affine independence remains necessary but is not sufficient. Unlike in the one-dimensional case, in environments with multidimensional states, extreme points can have uncountably many lower-dimensional components that are not singletons.

However, a key vulnerability of existing distributed learning approaches is their implicit assumption that all agents behave honestly during gradient updates. In real-world scenarios, this assumption often breaks down, as selfish or strategic agents may be incentivized to manipulate gradients for personal gain, ultimately compromising the final learning outcome. This represents a significant advancement, as it overcomes two major limitations of existing truthfulness mechanisms for collaborative learning:(1) reliance on a centralized server for payment collection, and (2) sacrificing convergence accuracy to guarantee truthfulness. Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.21163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robots, vehicles, and wearable devices often traverse the same environment many times. Each pass produces its own trajectory from onboard visual or visual-inertial odometry. These trajectories are locally accurate but drift over time and live in unrelated coordinate frames. Turning many such independent trajectories into one globally consistent set is the large-scale multi-session trajectory optimization problem. Existing solutions largely work offline. All sessions must be available up front, one session is fixed as the reference frame, and a single fused map is then optimized. This paper presents Polygraph, a multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that processes sessions online, one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time, and never builds a 3D map. Keyframes are grouped into local clusters. When a cluster closes, it is matched against every other session through learned image retrieval. Candidate pairs are verified with sparse feature matching, monocular metric depth, and robust pose estimation. A two-tier consensus gate admits a cross-session edge into the shared pose graph only once independent evidence corroborates it. A cheap incremental solve keeps the graph current, and a periodic robust batch solve prunes outliers. We evaluate Polygraph on stereo outdoor driving, HoloLens and iPad indoor traversals, legged indoor locomotion with a Boston Dynamics Spot, and large-scale outdoor vehicle and handheld routes. Against the closest prior work on the same GPU model, using its reported timings, Polygraph runs faster, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and matches or improves on accuracy.

arXiv:2611.22011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work we propose and analyze a procedure for estimating a generalized single-index regression model. This generalized single-index regression framework models the conditional mean of the responses $Y$ as a function of the covariates $X$ where the mapping is assumed to have the form $f \circ g$, where $g$ is $\beta$-H\"older with $\beta \geq 2$ and $f$ can be a discontinuous function of bounded variation. We propose a general procedure that operates under minimal assumptions about the distribution of covariates $X$, requiring only boundedness, sufficient smoothness and absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue. Our procedure jointly estimates the gradient vector $\hat v(x) \approx \nabla g(x)$ and the conditional mean $\mu(x) = f(g(x))$ by solving a localized weighted linear least squares problem. We derive central limit theorems for gradient vector estimates $\hat{v}_x$ and regression estimates $\hat{\mu}(x)$, and we derive rates of convergence for our approach, illustrating that it indeed achieves a stochastic convergence rate matching the minimax mean squared error rate when $\beta = 2$ and $f$ has a locally Lipschitz derivative. Unlike prior approaches our velocity estimation results accommodate link functions in the local bounded-variation class, allowing for nonsmooth and even discontinuous links while retaining consistency and asymptotic normality at almost every inference point. Finally, we instantiate this model in the situation where $g = \Pi$ is a closest point projection onto a compact and regular embedded $C^3$ curve $\gamma$, a setting recently studied in the literature. We also supplement our theoretical results with experiments on real and synthetic data to demonstrate the utility of our procedure.

But deliberately obscuring taxes may be viewed as dishonest. This creates a three-way trade-off between equality, efficiency, and honesty. We analyze this trade-off in a simple setting with a linear income tax. We define and characterize the morally efficient frontier, trading off utilitarian welfare against honesty or transparency. Complete honesty is Pareto inefficient but not morally inefficient. More generally, increasing honesty reduces utilitarian welfare. When utilitarian welfare is decomposed into equality and efficiency, the cost of honesty falls most robustly on equality: Higher salience always reduces equality, while the effect on efficiency is ambiguous. This asymmetry arises because salience increases the price of equality, which is the efficiency cost of a marginal increase in equality. Our approach could be applied to other settings in which utilitarian and procedural or deontological values conflict.

Relative camera pose is commonly estimated from matched image correspondences that satisfy the epipolar constraint; however, identifying geometrically consistent correspondences under varying imaging conditions remains challenging. We employ an existing detector-free transformer architecture to establish correspondences between image pairs and construct a correspondence graph whose topology is guided by epipolar geometry. Initially, each node is connected to its (k) nearest neighbours based on spatial distance. The resulting graph is subsequently pruned using an initial estimate of the Essential Matrix, distinguishing the proposed formulation from conventional graph representations based primarily on heuristic spatial neighbourhoods. The graph learning module aggregates relational information between nodes into a graph-level representation that encodes the geometric context of the correspondences. This representation is passed to a pose regression network to estimate the relative camera rotation and translation. The model is trained across standard and wide baselines using a weighted objective that combines pose regression, scale consistency, heading consistency, and spectral properties of the pose parameters. Experimental graph analyses demonstrate that epipolar-guided edge pruning reduces graph connectivity by more than 90\% while retaining all correspondence nodes. Further spectral analyses characterize the effects of graph sparsification and injected outliers on learned graph representations.

arXiv:2603.09589v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the memorization capacity of deep neural networks with ReLU activation. Specifically, we investigate the minimal size of such networks to memorize any $N$ data points in the unit ball with pairwise separation distance $\delta$ and labels from a finite set of size $C$. Most prior studies characterize the memorization capacity by the number of parameters or neurons. We extend these results by constructing ReLU networks with adjustable width $W$ and depth $L$ satisfying $W^2L^2\log W=\mathcal{O}(N(\log(\delta^{-1})+\log C))$ that can memorize any such dataset. We also establish width-depth lower bounds that depend explicitly on $\delta$ and $C$ for networks capable of memorizing all such datasets. When $\log(\delta^{-1})\asymp\log N$, our construction achieves $W^2L^2\asymp N$ for suitable choices of width and depth. This order is optimal if $\log C\asymp\log N$, and optimal up to logarithmic factors if $\log C=o(\log N)$.

The Economics of AI Foundation Models: Openness, Competition, and Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (295 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Sources indicate that arXiv:2510.15200v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation model developers choose how open to make their models. Greater openness lowers downstream adaptation costs but can also make competing models easier to use. In a two-period model, an incumbent chooses its license fee and openness, a deployer adapts the model for users, and an entrant offers a competing model. Usage builds model-specific experience that lowers the deployer's future adaptation cost, creating a data flywheel that favors continued use of the incumbent. We identify conditions under which optimal openness falls and then rises as learning strengthens. The incumbent moves from full openness and a high fee to restricting openness for retention, then to a low fee that builds enough usage and experience to retain the deployer despite greater openness. A full-openness mandate can induce the incumbent to abandon this low-fee strategy. The higher fee can reduce first-period adaptation despite greater openness. An openness trap arises when this welfare loss exceeds the second-period gain from easier adaptation of the entrant's model. The trap can disappear when experience transfers across models. Full integration eliminates the fee between the incumbent and deployer but commits deployment to the incumbent, potentially forgoing a rival that is cheaper to adapt. Integration raises their joint profit, consumer surplus, and welfare when learning is sufficiently strong, but can lower them when learning is weak. A small usage subsidy can benefit both developers, the deployer, and consumers. It can instead induce a fee increase larger than the subsidy and reduced openness, raising the deployer's net payment per use and adaptation costs. The resulting reduction in adaptation lowers welfare even before subsidy expenditure is deducted. These findings connect AI policy to developers' pricing and openness responses and the portability of deployment experience.

Randomizing the smaller (\emph{short}) side can reduce interference bias due to weaker competition, while randomizing the larger (\emph{long}) side provides a larger nominal sample, potentially reducing variance. On the surface, these competing considerations suggest a bias-variance trade-off in choosing which side to randomize. We investigate this trade-off in a two-sided marketplace with first-come, first-served (FCFS) booking and heterogeneous customer preferences, studying the bias and variance of difference-in-means estimators of the global average treatment effect. Our findings suggest that rather than a bias-variance tradeoff, in fact short-side randomization is generally preferable on {\em both} dimensions. We prove these results in an asymptotic regime where market imbalance increases. We establish conditions under which (1) short-side randomization eliminates first-order interference bias, while long-side randomization retains it; and (2) short-side randomization also achieves a variance rate of no larger asymptotic order than long-side randomization. The key insight is that although the long side contains more participants, the number of matches is constrained by the population on the short side, limiting the apparent variance advantage of randomizing a larger sample. Our conditions accommodate heterogeneous preferences and treatment effects and are satisfied by familiar logit models of customer choice. Together, these findings support randomizing on the short side, despite the larger sample size available on the long side.

Meanwhile, as training data in DRO always involves sensitive information, safeguarding it against leakage under Differential Privacy (DP) is essential. In contrast to classical DP-ERM, DP-DRO has received much less attention due to its minimax optimization structure with uncertainty constraint. To bridge the gap, we provide a comprehensive study of DP-(finite-sum)-DRO with $\psi$-divergence and non-convex loss. First, we study DRO with general $\psi$-divergence by reformulating it as a minimization problem, and develop a novel $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP optimization method, called DP Double-Spider, tailored to this structure. Under mild assumptions, we show that it achieves a utility bound of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+ (\frac{\sqrt{d \log (1/\delta)}}{n \varepsilon})^{2/3})$ in terms of the gradient norm, where $n$ denotes the data size and $d$ denotes the model dimension. We further improve the utility rate for specific divergences. In particular, for DP-DRO with KL-divergence, by transforming the problem into a compositional finite-sum optimization problem, we develop a DP Recursive-Spider method and show that it achieves a utility bound of $\mathcal{O}((\frac{\sqrt{d \log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3} )$, matching the best-known result for non-convex DP-ERM. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform existing approaches for DP minimax optimization.

arXiv:2611.21129v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: LLM agents can use remote tools and cloud sandboxes, but integrating reasoning, session state, and heterogeneous execution sites remains a runtime design problem. We present Linglong Agent Service (agentsvc), a self-hosted HTTP service and embeddable Python runtime that treats execution site as a configurable dimension alongside model, tools, and context. A parent service retains inference orchestration, tool descriptions, and conversation history; each inference request selects one child environment for file, shell, terminal, and MCP operations. Direct HTTP and child-initiated WebSocket tunnels carry the same application interfaces, including portable request context and centrally managed updates. The normal core path requires no third-party Python packages, with an optional Windows pseudo-terminal dependency. We further present online_debugger as the process-scale special case of execution-site separation: an instrumented program submits exception evidence, executes session-scoped inspection tools inside the incident process, and resumes the same diagnostic session. Its default prompt requires failing-then-passing reproduction evidence for source changes, while runtime patch activation and failed-call recovery remain unimplemented. We explain the design through constrained expected-utility reasoning, compare concrete mechanisms with Hermes Agent, Pi, Codex, and Claude Code, and report implementation and regression-test evidence. The current evidence establishes executable contracts, not performance advantages, repair accuracy, or production recovery. The source code is open source under the MIT license at https://github.com/mz24cn/agents.

#20981. Evercade Nexus Review: The Best Retro Handheld Yet

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1418 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Evercade Nexus Review: The Best Retro Handheld Yet

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Specialist hardware manufacturer Blaze Entertainment has spent the 2020s quietly carving out a niche for itself as the go-to option for retro gaming.
  • The Evercade Nexus is more than just the latest addition to its console lineup.
  • The most obvious change is the sheer size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Specialist hardware manufacturer Blaze Entertainment has spent the 2020s quietly carving out a niche for itself as the go-to option for retro gaming. With a stable of reliable hardware, from the original Evercade handheld to the Evercade Alpha bartop arcade cabinet, it offers numerous ways to play, all built around an ever-expanding library of physical cartridges. Each brings a curated selection of classic titles and lost curiosities to modern players.

The Evercade Nexus is more than just the latest addition to its console lineup. While it retains compatibility with every previously released Evercade cartridge, it’s also the biggest leap forward the line has taken so far, both in hardware and in what it might offer with games going forward. It’s a real level up—and it’s rather brilliant.

The most obvious change is the sheer size. Where Blaze’s previous handhelds were about on par with the original Game Boy Advance, aimed at pocketable play, the Evercade Nexus is closer in scale to a Nintendo Switch Lite. It measures 215 x 111 x 34 millimeters and weighs 410 grams—still easily portable, but more in the “buy a protective hard case and throw it in your bag” kind of way.

The size increase works in its favor, though. The larger design feels more substantial, with more real estate for your hands for better comfort. The control layout remains broadly the same as the Evercade EXP—a D-pad, ABXY face buttons, shoulder buttons, and triggers all return, with a few beneficial tweaks. Notably, the triggers are now chunkier and curved to meet your fingers, while all four shoulder inputs and the rear of the device are now nicely textured for better grip.

Recent findings suggest that the big change is the addition of twin symmetrical thumbsticks. This has implications for Evercade going forward—more on that later—but it also improves Tate Mode (pronounced tah-tay, meaning vertical in Japanese), a returning feature from the Evercade EXP. As on that model, tapping the dedicated mode-shift button rotates the screen 90 degrees, letting you play vertically scrolling arcade games in the intended orientation, rather than crammed into a tiny pillar-boxed view on the widescreen display.

Industry observers note that on the EXP, you’d hold the console on the left to use the D-pad for movement, which required duplicate A+B buttons on that side and cluttered the inputs. On the Nexus, Tate Mode rotates in the opposite direction, letting you use the right-hand thumbstick and the default ABXY buttons. It feels much better—again aided by the increased overall size—and keeps the device's design looking much tidier.

It has been revealed that whichever orientation you play in, the screen is bigger—a 5.89-inch IPS panel with an 840 × 512-pixel resolution for a 167 pixels-per-inch density, versus the original's 4.3-inch LCD—and brighter, now boasting 500-plus nits. It’s clear and colorful, and games look fantastic on it.

According to recent reports, the only minor build-quality demerits are the D-pad, which feels a little too raised and prone to rocking—a slightly more flush fit would have been better—and the glossy finish under the face buttons and around the front trim. These accents are aesthetically pleasing, standing out from the matte plastic of the rest of the unit, but they attract micro-scratches far too easily. Those small gripes aside, the Nexus is a huge improvement on its predecessors, feeling less like a quirky gadget and more like a serious, modern gaming handheld.

In a recent development, the Nexus doesn’t actually see any boosts in processor power or memory. It still uses the 1.5-GHz quad-core chip in the EXP with 512 MB of RAM. That may not sound like much in 2026, but it’s significantly more powerful than the original hardware it emulates, and it ensures Evercade’s universal cross-device compatibility for every cartridge.

Recent findings suggest that the downside is that the Nexus still feels slow at the system level. Booting it up takes about 35 to 40 seconds on average, and it can take about the same to load up a cartridge. Games don't have any performance challenges, but getting there is sluggish. Disappointingly, there’s also no quick-suspend feature, forcing you to power off fully and back on between play sessions.

There are some upgrades to the underlying tech, though. One material improvement is the battery, which jumped to a 5,000-mAh cell from the EXP's 3,000 mAh. Even with that bigger, brighter screen sucking up juice, the Nexus offers around five hours of play between charges, roughly an hour longer. On the audio front, the integrated front-facing stereo speakers are solid, offering louder, clearer output. Even better, the Nexus now supports Bluetooth, finally allowing you to connect wireless headphones, while still offering a 3.5-mm jack for wired headsets.

Bluetooth isn’t the only connectivity upgrade. The Nexus now supports the Wi-Fi 6 standard and can connect to 5-GHz networks (previous models could only use slower 2.4-GHz ones). That’s useful for downloading console updates and Evercade’s free Game of the Month. It also enables the fresh EverSync feature, unique to the Nexus, which allows multiple units to communicate wirelessly. Much like Nintendo’s GameShare, it’s set to allow multiplayer across devices even with only one cartridge, although I haven't been able to test this feature yet.

The underlying OS also gets a refresh. Hop into the settings menu and you'll find fresh customization tools. These let you adjust the color palette for the menu background and the glowing LED Nexus logo, select onscreen borders for non-widescreen games, and even tweak aspect ratios and virtual scan lines—all nice ways to personalize your device.

The glaring omission is any form of TV connectivity. Previous handheld Evercades featured a mini-HDMI out port, but that’s removed entirely here. It was always a nice-to-have rather than a major selling point, but it’s disappointing to lose a feature. Evercade players wanting TV play will have to opt for the Evercade VS-R set-top console.

Industry observers note that while the Nexus hardware is a significant improvement, more exciting is where the games themselves may be heading. Almost every game on Evercade to date has been from the 8-bit or 16-bit era, if not earlier, a period that near-universally consisted of 2D titles. Adding thumbsticks opens the door to an entirely upcoming generation of 3D games. Blaze says the Nexus works with 32- and 64-bit games, which dramatically expands possibilities for future releases.

More impressively, the first two cartridges to benefit from this generational leap also see Evercade step beyond emulation for the first time. Both the Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie double-pack and the DOOM and DOOM II collection are natively ported. That means improved performance, intentional widescreen aspect ratios to match the display, higher resolutions up to 60 frames per second, and on-cartridge save slots rather than virtual quick saves.

The Banjo duology is the real standout so far, with the colorful worlds of Rare’s classic 3D platformers shining on the Nexus’ superior screen while taking full advantage of the dual thumbsticks (something the N64 controller lacked) to offer smoother camera controls alongside free movement. These are authentic and accessible versions of 64-bit gaming greatness, without compromise. This might be the best way to play this pair of games, period, and all the better for being able to do so portably. (For anyone who’s looked up the price of a Banjo-Tooie cart on the secondary market, a bargain, too.) The DOOM collection also holds up well, with classic boomer shooters and a stack of bonus missions and map packs, but as some of the oldest examples of first-person shooters, they show their age more.

Sources indicate that the ports are to Evercade as an ecosystem, meaning the cartridges will still play on existing hardware—even Blaze’s budget Super Pocket devices—with camera controls mapped to shoulder buttons, albeit with a slower rotational view. It also partly explains the lack of power upgrades for the Nexus, as cross-device compatibility is a signature of the collection. Still, as Blaze works its way through gaming history, it feels as though a future Evercade will inevitably have to make a break to offer more power and support more recent games.

For now, though, the Nexus is hands-down the best way to play both Evercade’s vast library of games and this latest pseudo-generation of native releases. With its better screen, bigger form, and added controls for 3D games, it’s a delight to play on. If Blaze can keep up the momentum with more dedicated ports, this will be a bright new age for the best old games.

Despite steady progress in recognition accuracy, existing traffic sign datasets and benchmarks offer limited diagnostic insight into how different modeling paradigms behave under these practical challenges. We present TS-1M, a large-scale and globally diverse traffic sign dataset comprising over one million real-world images across 454 standardized categories, together with a diagnostic benchmark designed to analyze model capability boundaries. Beyond standard train-test evaluation, we provide a suite of challenge-oriented settings, including cross-region recognition, rare-class identification, low-clarity robustness, and semantic text understanding, enabling systematic and fine-grained assessment of modern TSR models. Using TS-1M, we conduct a unified benchmark across three representative learning paradigms: classical supervised models, self-supervised pretrained models, and multimodal vision-language models (VLMs). Our analysis reveals consistent paradigm-dependent behaviors, showing that semantic alignment is a key factor for cross-region generalization and rare-category recognition, while purely visual models remain sensitive to appearance shift and data imbalance. Finally, we validate the practical relevance of TS-1M through real-scene autonomous driving experiments, where traffic sign recognition is integrated with semantic reasoning and spatial localization to support map-level decision constraints. Overall, TS-1M establishes a reference-level diagnostic benchmark for TSR and provides principled insights into robust and semantic-aware traffic sign perception. arXiv:2609.00541v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In a network with ramp-limited generators and inaccurate net-demand forecasts, practical rolling-window dispatch can drive locational marginal prices (LMPs) below generators' bid-in offers. In such cases, out-of-market (OOM) settlements are used to compensate generators and maintain dispatch-following incentives, but OOM can have negative consequences, including nontransparent real-time price signals, discriminatory compensation, and incentives for untruthful bidding. This paper presents an optimal uniform pricing rule that minimizes demand payments, eliminates OOM make-whole payments, preserves LMP-based congestion charges, and ensures revenue adequacy. We derive the proposed pricing rule in closed form and relate it to existing pricing schemes. Numerical comparisons demonstrate favorable generator profits and reduced price volatility. However, higher generator profits are accompanied by increased demand payments, reflecting the in-market, uniform allocation of ramping costs while preserving the LMP-based congestion charges widely used in real-time market settlements. The numerical results also show that, under LMP with OOM settlement, a price-taking generator has an incentive to inflate its offer, whereas this incentive is absent under the proposed pricing rule within the tested bid range.

Retrieval makes no language-model call, indexing makes one per passage, and deleting a document is a database transaction with no model calls: 14 seconds for 10% of an 11,402-passage corpus, after which the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. Seeding the walk from entities named in the question accounts for most of the 2WikiMultiHopQA gain. Answers tie on all three datasets, and the retrieval pattern holds with three larger embedders, up to Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The gain is not the reranker's: with the same cross-encoder, dense retrieval trails Lightfoot by 9.3 and 17.8 points recall@5 on the two multi-hop sets. Lightfoot also builds the cheapest index, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2; LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours for the same deletion, and fast-graphrag cannot delete.

arXiv:2605.09079v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite surpassing human performance across mathematics, coding, and other knowledge-intensive tasks, large language models (LLMs) continue to struggle with causal reasoning. A core obstacle is the target data itself: causal systems are complex and often expressed in non-executable forms, while ground-truth answers to causal queries are inherently scarce. We introduce CauSim, a framework that turns causal reasoning from a scarce-label problem into a scalable supervised one. CauSim constructs increasingly complex causal simulators: executable structural causal models (SCMs), incrementally built by LLMs, that scale to globally complex systems while maintaining verifiable answers to causal queries. CauSim operates across representations by formalizing non-executable causal knowledge into code, enabling data augmentation, and translating executable SCMs into natural language, enabling supervision in previously difficult-to-supervise representations. We structure our research into two parts: (1) how to construct increasingly complex causal simulators, and (2) a systematic study of what CauSim enables, demonstrating generalization across representations, consistent gains from curriculum scaling and data volume, LLM self-improvement through self-generated simulators, and data augmentation via formalization of existing domain knowledge.

arXiv:2611.21099v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.

Settling the Time and Structural Complexity of Bertrand Networks

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (256 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22216v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the seminal Bertrand network game introduced by Babaioff et al. (2013), each seller posts a single price to captive buyers and to the markets it shares with neighboring sellers, where sellers cannot price discriminate across the markets. Although the existence of equilibria and polynomial-time algorithms to compute them in trees (Babaioff et al. (2013)) have been known, it has been a major open problem whether there exist efficient algorithms to compute them for general graphs. In this paper, we resolve this open question negatively by proving that computing any constant-error approximate Nash equilibrium in a Bertrand network is $\PPAD$-complete. This hardness holds even on sparse bipartite graphs of maximum degree five with constant integer market weights. Complementing our hardness result, we design an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPTAS) when both the maximum degree and the number of sellers with captive buyers are bounded. Beyond time complexity, since exact equilibria require randomizing prices over continuous intervals, another fundamental question left open by Babaioff et al. (2013) is whether an exact equilibrium can always be represented with a finite number of price intervals, \ie whether its structural complexity is finite. We resolve this question affirmatively by proving that every achievable equilibrium revenue profile can be realized by an equilibrium with structural complexity $O(2^n)$, which leads to an exact algorithm running in doubly exponential time. We further show that this bound is tight: there exist instances for which the unique equilibrium realizing target revenue profiles has structural complexity $\Omega(2^n)$.

The diagnosis reveals a developer which stage to improve and directs test-time compute to the stage that fails. Benchmarks score the final answer, and an answer that rests on the image earns the same credit as a guess or a memorized prior. The protocol asks the model two extra questions per item and needs no access to its weights. A localization probe asks for a box around every instance and measures seeing, and a text-replacement probe answers from a description and measures thinking. Use is the rate at which the answer follows the model's own perception across counterfactual image pairs. The rate needs no answer labels, because the question and its prior are the same on both images. On two model families and six datasets the protocol shows that the knob that helps follows the task family. Answers follow the model's perception except on images that contradict a common prior, and asking the model to localize first repairs this failure when its boxes are right. Allocating compute by the measured stages comes close to the best uniform policy at lower cost and beats a random allocation of the same compute wherever a knob raises the short stage. We will release the code, the prompts and the per-question outputs.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2602.05459v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) methods are typically benchmarked by the success rates of optimized hyperparameter configurations. However, success rate by itself does not provide information about the sensitivity of algorithms to hyperparameters for value learning or policy extraction, since an algorithm could obtain the same success rate across a wide range of hyperparameters, or might succeed only on specific settings. We study this phenomenon in the offline GCRL algorithms GCIQL, GCIVL, QRL, and CRL under a shared policy extractor, by constructing landscapes of interaction between the learning rate and policy extraction hyperparameters such as the temperature of advantage-weighted regression (AWR). These landscapes reveal large, task-dependent differences in hyperparameter sensitivity. On AntMaze-M, 59% of QRL configurations and 66% of CRL configurations achieve at least 90% of the method's best sampled success rate, compared with 3% for both GCIQL and GCIVL. On Cube and Scene, GCIQL and GCIVL instead attain higher success over broader hyperparameter regions than QRL and CRL. To interpret these differences, we analyze how reliably learned advantages rank actual goals from the same trajectory above random goals, and how strongly AWR concentrates policy updates on a small subset of transitions. Our findings indicate strongly differing behavior of these algorithms at policy-extraction time, even under the same success rates. Given these results, we argue that offline GCRL methods should be evaluated by both attainable success and the needed hyperparameter range to sustain it, complemented by post-hoc diagnostics to understand the signal used to train the policy. The overview and code are available at https://luh-ai.github.io/GCRL-Landscapes/ .

Driving world models have shown great potential in learning rich representations by predicting the future evolution of a driving scene. However, existing driving world models primarily focus on visual scene representation, and motion representation is not explicitly designed to be planner-shared and inheritable, leaving a schism between the optimization of visual scene generation and the requirements of precise motion planning. We present WorldDrive, a holistic framework that couples scene generation and real-time planning via unifying vision and motion representation. We first introduce a Trajectory-aware Driving World Model, which conditions on a trajectory vocabulary to enforce consistency between visual dynamics and motion intentions, enabling the generation of diverse and plausible future scenes conditioned on a specific trajectory. We transfer the vision and motion encoders to a downstream Multi-modal Planner, ensuring the driving policy operates on mature representations pre-optimized by scene generation. A simple interaction between motion representation, visual representation, and ego status can generate high-quality, multi-modal trajectories. Furthermore, to exploit the world model's foresight, we propose a Future-aware Rewarder, which distills future latent representation from the frozen world model to evaluate and select optimal trajectories in real-time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WorldDrive achieves leading planning performance among vision-only methods while maintaining high-fidelity action-controlled video generation capabilities.

However, existing RLVR approaches typically rely on outcome-driven optimization that updates both perception and reasoning using a shared reward based solely on the final answer. This shared reward blurs credit assignment, frequently improving reasoning patterns while failing to reliably enhance the accuracy of upstream visual evidence extraction. To address this perception bottleneck, we introduce PRCO (Perception-Reasoning Coevolution), a dual-role RLVR framework with a shared policy. PRCO consists of two cooperative roles: an Observer that generates an evidence caption tailored to the question and a Solver that predicts the final answer based on this caption. Crucially, PRCO employs role-specific reward signals: the Solver is optimized using verifiable outcome rewards on the final answer, while the Observer receives a utility reward derived from the Solver's downstream success. Extensive experiments across eight challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that PRCO yields consistent improvements across model scales by over 7 points on average accuracy compared to the base model, outperforming prior open-source RL-tuned baselines.

#20956. AI DJs Completely Kill My Groove

AI DJs Completely Kill My Groove

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I usually can’t pinpoint the moment I stop using a software feature, with most tools drifting out of fashion without an expiration date.
  • It has been revealed that youTube Music is my music-streaming service of choice.
  • More listeners are encountering synthetic commentary built into their music streaming apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I usually can’t pinpoint the moment I stop using a software feature, with most tools drifting out of fashion without an expiration date. That’s not the case with YouTube Music’s “Beyond the Beat,” an AI-generated DJ that explains songs to you.

It has been revealed that youTube Music is my music-streaming service of choice. And since I’m a software reporter, I always enable the beta features available through YouTube Labs, which include Beyond the Beat. YouTube’s AI DJ randomly interjects for about 30 seconds between songs, teeing up the vibe shift and providing context about the next track.

More listeners are encountering synthetic commentary built into their music streaming apps. While YouTube debuted this experimental AI DJ in 2025, Spotify first introduced a similar tool back in 2023. It doubled down on its AI DJ efforts in November, expanding the different personalities available to consumers and adding more controls over the commentary.

These AI DJs aren’t just annoying. Their attempts to provide helpful context and mimic human candor ultimately fall flat. Lucky for me, both features are optional and avoidable.

It has been revealed that after months of leaving it enabled, a bad experience with Beyond the Beat this week pushed me to swear off AI DJs altogether. I was listening to a pop divas playlist as part of my morning workout and got slapped with 30 seconds of exposition after a Slayyyter track:.

“Hey Boy delivers that high-energy surge perfectly, but we're shifting our focus to a sharper, more visceral reality. In Rock Music, Charli XXC [sic] weaves in a biting, dark sense of humor regarding the physical toll of her relentless 2024 and 2025 touring. She turns the genuine nerve damage she sustained on the road into a strange sort of battle scar, reclaiming the exhaustion of a weary party girl as a badge of honor. It's an unflinching look at the cost behind the spectacle, where the grind of the industry becomes the actual subject matter. Here is Rock Music by Charli XXC [sic].”.

It has been revealed that what a lengthy paragraph of platitudes with little substance. That’s not even mentioning how the AI DJ butchered the pronunciation of a little-known, indie act called Charli XCX. This flub reflected my overall experience with YouTube Music’s AI DJ. It took me out of the groove and didn’t feel additive.

In another example, it went in-depth on the meaning of Olivia Rodrigo’s Expectations remix featuring Chappell Roan, calling it a "structural interpretation” that unpacks the “nuances of queer dating.” Then YouTube Music played the original track, sans Roan; so much for the queer yearning.

It has been revealed that curious how Spotify’s AI DJ experience would compare, I upgraded my account to the premium tier for access to that beta software. One of the biggest recent changes to Spotify’s AI DJ was adding fresh voices to the lineup, so I went into my settings and played the introduction clips for each of the eight English-language voices.

In a recent development, maybe I was already a bit miffed from my YouTube Music experience because these voices immediately started to frustrate me. Multiple voices leaned into filler words such as “you know” and “like,” as the AI described the next songs it would play. Knowing an AI voice is being trained to use filler words to sound more human gave me the uncanny-valley ick.

Sources indicate that spotify’s AI DJ was fairly different from YouTube Music’s version. On Spotify, the AI DJ is also an algorithmically guided experience that picks songs for you based on past listening habits and song requests. Overall, Spotify’s synthetic commentary felt tighter and more tolerable than YouTube’s blabbering DJ. That said, neither software experience was enjoyable enough for me to return.

Industry observers note that although Spotify claims it has “80 percent of listeners coming back to DJ week after week,” according to the tech giant’s launch blog, I won’t be one of them. My rejection of AI DJs isn’t based on how they audibly sound. The voices, from both companies, are decent and sound convincingly human. The content of their commentary is what truly turns me off. Whether it’s empty platitudes or mimicking human mistakes, I’ve heard enough.

arXiv:2105.09254v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In many applications, researchers are interested in the direct and indirect causal effects of a treatment or exposure on an outcome of interest. Mediation analysis offers a rigorous framework for identifying and estimating these causal effects. For binary treatments, efficient estimators for the direct and indirect effects are presented by Tchetgen Tchetgen and Shpitser (2012) based on the influence function of the parameter of interest. These estimators possess desirable properties such as multiple-robustness and asymptotic normality while allowing for slower than root-n rates of convergence for the nuisance parameters. However, in settings involving continuous treatments, these influence function-based estimators are not readily applicable without making strong parametric assumptions. In this work, utilizing a kernel smoothing approach, we propose an estimator suitable for settings with continuous treatments inspired by the influence function-based estimation strategy. Our proposed approach employs cross-fitting, relaxing the smoothness requirements on the nuisance functions and allowing them to be estimated at slower rates than the target parameter. Additionally, similar to influence function-based estimators, our proposed estimator is multiply robust and asymptotically normal, allowing for inference in settings where parametric assumptions may not be justified.

We show that under a single-peakedness condition on private beliefs a larger payoff both increases the probability of an incorrect consensus on the favored account and reduces its reliability. arXiv:2603.01608v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As frontier language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents pursuing complex, long-term objectives, there is increased risk of scheming: agents covertly pursuing misaligned goals. Prior work has focused on showing agents are capable of scheming, but their propensity to scheme in realistic scenarios remains underexplored. To understand when agents scheme, we decompose scheming incentives into agent factors and environmental factors. We develop realistic settings allowing us to systematically vary these factors, each with scheming opportunities for agents that pursue instrumentally convergent goals such as self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal-guarding. Across 11 frontier models and four scenarios, we find almost no scheming despite high environmental incentives, and show this is unlikely to be explained by verbalized evaluation awareness. While inserting adversarially-designed prompt snippets that encourage agency and goal-directedness into an agent's system prompt can induce high scheming rates, snippets used in real agent scaffolds rarely do. In model organisms built with these snippets, scheming behavior is brittle: removing a single tool can drop the scheming rate from 59% to 3%. Increasing oversight can raise rather than deter scheming by up to 25%, an effect that depends on the wording of the oversight sentence and does not appear in a second scenario, where the sabotage itself is reviewed. These results suggest that scheming propensity should be reported per agent configuration rather than as a single rate. Our incentive decomposition enables such systematic measurement in settings relevant for deployment, which is necessary as agents are entrusted with increasingly consequential tasks.

Earlier display attracts more trials but can retain a smaller fraction of them. For small positive losses, assigning return costs to consumers raises the value of prominence relative to reimbursing firms by the same amount. In markets with frequent returns, the platform can instead share the bill with consumers: a higher commission makes it pay more to encourage shopping and retained sales. Results at finite losses show that advertising can change the optimal policy from firm-paid free returns to full consumer payment, reducing both commissions and consumer surplus. 📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (263 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2610.02001v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Small open-weight language models now run on a laptop, but they fail at multi-step work in ways a large model does not: they stop with the files missing, repeat one action until the budget ends, and report success without checking. At the one-to-nine-billion-parameter tier the harness supplies almost all of the procedural control that a large model supplies for itself.We present Mingbird, an open-source harness for that tier on a consumer graphics card: 12k lines of Python, a 628-test suite, and eighteen mechanisms for context economy, completion, time budget and the host boundary, plus a crawl guard outside those four groups. Its design point is completion control: the harness runs executable checks on the working directory and refuses a claim of completion when they fail.Five evaluations accompany it. A configuration-surface audit finds four defects that the 625-test suite of v3.1.1 missed, each because a test checked a property adjacent to the one that broke. A ten-task probe suite gives each mechanism a reason to fire and reports where the change reaches the artifact, including one mechanism that cuts the signal it protects. Disabling five of six completion-time checks costs 0.152 of the artifact score on eighteen held-out tasks, three replications per cell (95% CI [+0.064, +0.246], Holm p = 0.014). On a 288-cell matrix the harness reaches 0.886 against 0.631, 0.479 and 0.405 for three open scaffolds, and on {\tau} 2 -bench it ranks first or tied first in all three domains against the arms evaluated.Tasks, scorer, source and every per-cell result are public.

Multi-CONDOR: Learning Multistable Motion Primitives from Demonstration

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (235 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21059v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Dynamical-system-based motion policies provide a framework for learning reactive robot motions with stability and convergence properties. Many manipulation tasks, however, admit several distinct goals or a continuous set of acceptable outcomes, requiring motion primitives that preserve these alternatives. Accommodating both goal structures within a unified framework with continuous, autonomous dynamics remains an open challenge. We propose a CONDOR-based framework, multi-CONDOR, for learning motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour. The approach combines imitation learning with losses that encourage agreement between the learned task dynamics and latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure. We provide a Lyapunov-based analysis of the convergence properties of the learned motion dynamics. We evaluate the framework on simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, qualitative examples with continuous goal contours, and robotic grasping experiments. In simulation, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared with separately learned single-goal motion primitives selected by a state machine. For tasks with two and three goals, respectively, it reduces the fraction of evaluated initial states ending outside the goal tolerance from StableNODE's 0.31% and 7.29% to 0% in both settings. Experiments with a Franka Emika robot arm demonstrate successful grasping of a container by either of its two handles using motions learned from demonstrations. Together, these results show multi-CONDOR combines motion reproduction with the flexibility to converge to alternative valid outcomes.

Functional Compression as Occam's Razor: Algebraic Complexity from Sensitivity Minimization

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (263 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2511.23152v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discovering discrete algebraic structures from data is a fundamental challenge in machine learning. We ask how continuous learning objectives can favor functional compression---representing data through shared algebraic composition rather than low-rank representations. We analyze the global optima of a canonical factorization model for algebraic completion (recovering finite binary operations) that demonstrated a preference for group operations. We measure algebraic complexity by the infimum of parameter sensitivity under exact reconstruction. We establish a universal complexity floor, whose attainment forces geometric alignment and unitarity of the latent representations. At the floor, input representations compose into the corresponding output representations; their reuse across the operation table propagates these local identities to enforce a globally shared algebraic structure. If the floor is not attained, a positive gap separates it from the feasible infimum. For cancellative operations, floor attainment forces the model's latent representation to be an injective homomorphism, equivalent to the target being isotopic to a group. In this case, every global minimizer is equivalent to the underlying group's unitary left-regular representation, up to isotopy and unitary gauge, resolving the central conjecture of Huh (2025). For non-cancellative operations, floor attainment forces exact structural redundancies (identical rows or columns) and is equivalent to a unitary factorization of the target's row- and column-reduced table with orthonormal output matrices, yielding the fewest distinct input matrices compatible with exact reconstruction. The resulting cancellative table then embeds in a group-isotope table. This analysis reveals a structural bias toward functional compression: at the sensitivity floor, algebraic composition of latent representations implements the target operation.

Tech Report: Reserve Systems in Dynamic Settings: Account Design and Inherited Rights

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (243 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22116v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Research on reserve systems mainly considers static settings, formulating and studying choice rules for a given allocation problem. Dynamic settings are different in that the problem is not given. Over time, more positions become available, and each time the institution must build the current problem from its past. We distinguish the ledger, which stores information about earlier allocations, the account, which transforms these data into the current problem, and the choice rule, which selects an outcome for that problem. The same choice rule can implement very different policies under different accounts. If each new batch is assigned while holding earlier recipients and their categories fixed, then as batches shrink, over-and-above, the most generous reserve policy we study, can select nearly the same recipients as minimum guarantee, the most conservative one. Cumulative implementation uses a different account, which reconsiders the categories of earlier recipients, and prevents this compression. We characterize it by resource-release invariance. With arrivals or changes in priorities, the ordinary choice rule might reject an earlier recipient whose appointment has to be honored. We introduce and characterize retain, reassign, and boost (RRB) choice rules, under which every incumbent retains her appointment and can have her category changed. Combining RRB with individual-proposing deferred acceptance gives a strategy-proof mechanism under which each incumbent keeps her appointment or receives one she prefers. Applications include waiting lists in school and university admissions, public recruitment, and court-ordered corrections.
